description: Semantic version ordering, and the update window a licence's maxVersion describes. Hand written: this is the specification, and generating it from an implementation would only prove that the implementation agrees with itself.
notes: 'compare' cases give an expected sign: -1 when left orders below right, 0 when equal, 1 when above.
Build metadata after '+' is ignored entirely, so two versions differing only there compare equal.
A pre-release orders BELOW the release it precedes. 2.0.0-rc.1 is not yet 2.0.0.
'within' cases are the licence question: may a build of appVersion run under a licence capped at maxVersion? Null on either side means yes - see the reasoning in semver.ts / semver.py.
'parse' cases pin what counts as a version at all. Anything that does not parse must not lock a paying customer out.

compare.why: A missing minor or patch is zero, not absent. '1' and '1.0.0' are the same release.
Half the world writes tags with a v. Refusing it would refuse the version it allows.
SemVer 2.0.0: build metadata is not part of precedence. Two builds of the same version are the same version.
2.0.0 outranks 1.99.99 - the whole point of the major number.
THE reason this module exists. As strings '1.10.0' < '1.9.0'; as versions it is the other way round, and the mistake only surfaces at the tenth minor release.
The same trap one order of magnitude further on, where a naive fix that pads to two digits also breaks.
The same trap in the third component, which is where it actually happens first.
2.0.0-rc.1 is not yet 2.0.0. A licence capped at 1.9.9 must block both; a licence capped at 2.0.0 must allow the release candidate.
The pre-release rule only applies within the same numbers. 2.0.0-alpha is still above 1.9.9.
beta.2 comes before beta.10, which is exactly the trap the release numbers have.
SemVer 2.0.0 rule 11.4.1. Reads backwards until you remember that 'alpha' is a word and '1' is a build counter.
alpha < beta < rc, which is the convention every release process here uses.
SemVer 2.0.0 rule 11.4.4. More identifiers means more specific, so 1.0.0-alpha comes before 1.0.0-alpha.1.
The example in the specification itself, one step of it, so a rewrite that gets the individual rules right but composes them wrongly still fails.
Metadata is stripped before the pre-release is compared, not after.

within.why: A subscription has no update window. There is nothing to be past.
An empty string is a null that went through a form. Same answer.
'Up to and including' - a licence for 2.4.0 covers 2.4.0. An off-by-one here locks out everybody who bought the current release.
The ordinary case for a perpetual licence: an older build keeps working forever.
The whole point. A perpetual licence sold for the 2.x line does not cover 3.0.
The window is a version, not a major line.
The string-comparison trap, in the form that actually reaches a customer: a licence capped at 1.9.0 must not silently cover 1.10.0.
2.4.0-rc.1 orders below 2.4.0, so a licence capped at 2.4.0 covers its own release candidates.
A beta of 3.0 is still a build of 3.0, and the licence stops at 2.x.
A build reporting 'dev' or a commit hash is a developer's build or a repackaged distribution. Neither is a licence violation, and the server enforces the same window with data the client cannot edit.
That is our own data being wrong. Locking a paying customer out over a malformed field in our database would be indefensible.
A caller that does not know its own version gets no answer rather than a wrong one.
A CI build stamp must not turn an allowed version into a refused one.
The licence was typed by a human into an admin form; the version comes from a build script. They will not agree on the v.

parse.why: '2' is a version. Some products really do ship one number.
A version read out of a file usually arrives with a newline on it.
Numeric identifiers become numbers so they compare numerically; the rest stay strings.
Not SemVer. Windows file versions look like this and must not be guessed at.
A dangling hyphen is a typo, not a pre-release.
What an unversioned build actually reports.
